items.topic: Absence of geometrical isomerism in tetrahedral complexes

prompt.text: Why is geometrical isomerism not possible in tetrahedral complexes having two different types of unidentate ligands coordinated with the central metal ion?

flow.text: Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism. This is because the unidentate ligands attached to the central metal atom always have the same relative positions with respect to each other.

prompt.text: The spin only magnetic moment of $\left[\mathrm{MnBr}_{4}\right]^{2-}$ is 5.9 BM. Predict the geometry of the complex ion ?

flow.text: The coordination number of $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ ion in the complex ion is 4. So the complex ion will be either tetrahedral ( $s p^{3}$ hybridisation) or square planar ( $d s p^{2}$ hybridisation).

The magnetic moment of the complex ion is 5.9 BM. This value matches five unpaired electrons in the $d$ orbitals. A tetrahedral shape allows five unpaired electrons, but a square planar shape does not.
So the complex ion is tetrahedral in shape, not square planar.

prompt.text: Explain the bonding in coordination compounds in terms of Werner's postulates.

flow.text:
Werner's postulates explain the bonding in coordination compounds as follows:

(i) A metal shows two types of valencies: primary and secondary. Negative ions satisfy primary valencies. Both negative ions and neutral molecules can satisfy secondary valencies.
(In modern terms, primary valency is the oxidation number of the metal ion. Secondary valency is the coordination number of the metal ion.

(ii) A metal ion has a fixed number of secondary valencies around the central atom. These valencies point in specific directions in space, giving the coordination compound its definite geometry.
(iii) Primary valencies are usually ionizable. Secondary valencies are non-ionizable.

tetraamminocopper(ii) sulphate
Both $\quad \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ and $\left[\mathrm{Cu}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{4}\right] \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ are addition compounds. The only major difference is that the former is a double salt, while the latter is a coordination compound.

A double salt is an addition compound. It is stable in the solid state, but breaks up into its constituent ions when dissolved. These compounds show the individual properties of their constituents. For example, $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ breaks into $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}, \mathrm{NH}^{4+}$ and $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ ions. So it gives a positive test for $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions. A coordination compound is an addition compound that keeps its identity both in the solid state and in solution. prompt.text: Explain with two examples each of the following: coordination entity, ligand, coordination number, coordination polyhedron, homoleptic and heteroleptic.

flow.text:
Ligands

Neutral molecules or negatively charged ions that surround the metal atom in a coordination entity or a coordinal complex are called ligands. For example,
$\ddot{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{H}_{3}, \mathrm{H}_{2} \ddot{\mathrm{O}}, \mathrm{Cl}^{-},-\mathrm{OH}$. Ligands are usually polar and have at least one unshared pair of valence electrons.

Coordination number:

The coordination number of a metal atom is the total number of ligands (neutral molecules or negative ions) attached to it in the coordination sphere. It is also called its ligancy.

For example:

(a) In the complex $\mathrm{K}_{2}\left[\mathrm{PtCl}_{6}\right]$, six chloride ions are attached to Pt in the coordination sphere. So the coordination number of Pt is 6.
(b) Similarly, in the complex $\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{4}\right] \mathrm{Cl}_{2}$, the coordination number of the central atom $(\mathrm{Ni})$ is 4.

Coordination polyhedron:

The coordination polyhedron is the spatial arrangement of the ligands that are directly attached to the central metal ion in the coordination sphere. For example:



Tetrahedral

Homoleptic complexes:

These are complexes in which the metal ion is bound to only one kind of donor group. For example: $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]^{3+},\left[\mathrm{PtCl}_{4}\right]^{2-}$ etc.

Heteroleptic complexes:

These are complexes in which the central metal ion is bound to more than one type of donor group.

For example: $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{4} \mathrm{Cl}_{2}\right]^{+},\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5} \mathrm{Cl}\right]^{2+}$

flow.text: Unidentate ligands: Ligands with only one donor site are called unidentate ligands. For example, ${ } \ddot{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{H}_{3}, \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ etc.

Didentate ligands: Ligands that have two donor sites are called didentate ligands. For e.g.,
(a) Ethane-1,2-diamine

(b) Oxalate ion

Ambidentate ligands:

Ligands that can attach themselves to the central metal atom through two different atoms are called ambidentate ligands. For example:

prompt.text: List various types of isomerism possible for coordination compounds, giving an example of each.

flow.text:
(a) Geometric isomerism:

This type of isomerism is common in heteroleptic complexes. It arises because the ligands can have different possible geometric arrangements. For example:

Cis-isomer

Trans-isomer

(b) Optical isomerism:

This type of isomerism arises in chiral molecules. The isomers are mirror images of each other, and they cannot be superimposed on one another.

(c) Linkage isomerism: This type of isomerism is found in complexes that contain ambidentate ligands. For example:
$\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5}\left(\mathrm{NO}_{2}\right)\right] \mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ and $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5}(\mathrm{ONO}) \mathrm{Cl}_{2}\right.$
Yellow form Red form (d)

Coordination isomerism:
This type of isomerism arises when ligands are interchanged between the cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in the complex.
$\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]\left[\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}\right]$ and $\left[\mathrm{Cr}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}\right](\mathbf{e})$

Ionization isomerism:
This type of isomerism arises when a counter ion replaces a ligand within the coordination sphere. So complexes with the same composition, but that give different ions when dissolved in water, are called ionization isomers. For example,
$\left.\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5} \mathrm{SO}_{4}\right) \mathrm{Br}$ and $\left.\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5} \mathrm{Br}\right] \mathrm{SO}_{4}$.

(f) Solvate isomerism:
Solvate isomers differ in whether the solvent molecule is directly bonded to the metal ion, or is simply present as a free solvent molecule in the crystal lattice.
$\left[\mathrm{Cr}\left[\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right] \mathrm{Cl}_{3}\left[\mathrm{Cr}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{5} \mathrm{Cl}\right] \mathrm{Cl}_{2} . \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\left[\mathrm{Cr}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{5} \mathrm{Cl}_{2}\right] \mathrm{Cl} .2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

prompt.text: Draw figure to show the splitting of $d$ orbitals in an octahedral crystal field.

flow.text: In an octahedral field, the $d$ orbitals split so that $d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}$ and $d_{z^{2}}$ rise in energy and form the $e_{g}$ level, while $d_{x y}, d_{y z}$ and $d_{z x}$ fall in energy and form the $t_{2 g}$ level.

prompt.text: What is spectrochemical series? Explain the difference between a weak field ligand and a strong field ligand.

flow.text: A spectrochemical series arranges common ligands in increasing order of their crystal-field splitting energy (CFSE) values. Ligands on the right-hand side of the series are strong field ligands. Ligands on the left-hand side are weak field ligands. Strong field ligands cause more splitting in the $d$ orbitals than weak field ligands.

prompt.text: What is crystal field splitting energy? How does the magnitude of $\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}$ decide the actual configuration of $d$ orbitals in a coordination entity?

flow.text: The degenerate $d$-orbitals (in a spherical field environment) split into two levels, $e_{g}$ and $t_{2 \mathrm{~g}}$, when ligands are present. This splitting is called crystal-field splitting. The energy difference between the two levels ( $e_{\mathrm{g}}$ and $t_{2 \mathrm{~g}}$ ) is called the crystal-field splitting energy. It is denoted by $\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}$.

After the orbitals split, electrons start filling them. First, 1 electron each fills the three $t_{2 \mathrm{~g}}$ orbitals. Then the fourth electron can go in two ways: it can enter the $e_{\mathrm{g}}$ orbital, giving an $t_{2 \mathrm{~g}}{ }^{3} e_{\mathrm{g}}{ }^{1}$-like electronic configuration, or it can pair up in the $t_{2 g}$ orbitals, giving an $t_{2 g}{ }^{4} e_{g}{ }^{0}$-like electronic configuration. If the $\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}$ value of a ligand is less than the pairing energy ( P ), the electron enters the $e_{\mathrm{g}}$ orbital. If the $\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}$ value of a ligand is more than the pairing energy (P), the electron enters the $t_{2 \mathrm{~g}}$ orbital.

prompt.text: $\left[\mathrm{Cr}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]^{3+}$ is paramagnetic while $\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}\right]^{2-}$ is diamagnetic. Explain why?

flow.text:
Cr is in the +3 oxidation state, i.e., $d^{3}$ configuration. Also, $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ is a weak field ligand. It does not cause pairing of electrons in the $3 d$ orbital. $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$

So it undergoes $d^{2} s p^{3}$ hybridization, and the electrons in the $3 d$ orbitals stay unpaired. Hence, it is paramagnetic.

In $\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}\right]^{2-}$, Ni is in the +2 oxidation state, i.e., $d^{8}$ configuration.
$\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$



$\mathrm{CN}^{-}$ is a strong field ligand. It causes pairing of the $3 d$ orbital electrons. Then $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ undergoes $d s p^{2}$ hybridization.

As there are no unpaired electrons, it is diamagnetic.

prompt.text: A solution of $\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}$ is green but a solution of $\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}\right]^{2-}$ is colourless. Explain.

flow.text: In $\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}$, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \ddot{\mathrm{O}}$ is a weak field ligand. So there are unpaired electrons in $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$. In this complex, the $d$ electrons can be excited from the lower energy level to the higher energy level, i.e., $d-d$ transition is possible. Hence, $\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}$ is coloured. In $\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}\right]^{2-}$, all the electrons are paired because $\mathrm{CN}^{-}$ is a strong field ligand. So $d-d$ transition is not possible in $\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_{4}\right]^{2-}$. Hence, it is colourless.

prompt.text: $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}\right]^{4-}$ and $\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}$ are of different colours in dilute solutions. Why?

flow.text: The colour of a coordination compound depends on the magnitude of the crystal-field splitting energy, $\Delta$. This CFSE in turn depends on the nature of the ligand. In the case of $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}\right]^{4-}$ and $\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}$, the colour differs because the CFSE differs. prompt.text: Discuss the nature of bonding in metal carbonyls.

figures.caption: Synergic bonding in metal carbonyls

flow.text: The metal-carbon bonds in metal carbonyls have both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character. A $\sigma$ bond forms when the carbonyl carbon donates a lone pair of electrons to a vacant orbital on the metal. A $\pi$ bond forms when a pair of electrons from the filled metal $d$ orbital is donated into the vacant anti-bonding $\pi^{*}$ orbital (this is also called back bonding of the carbonyl group). The $\sigma$ bond strengthens the $\pi$ bond, and vice versa. This creates a synergic effect from the metal-ligand bonding, which strengthens the bond between CO and the metal.

prompt.text: Discuss briefly giving an example in each case the role of coordination compounds in:

flow.text:
Role of coordination compounds in biological systems:

Photosynthesis happens because of the chlorophyll pigment, which is a coordination compound of magnesium. In the human body too, several coordination compounds play important roles. For example, haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrier in blood, is a coordination compound of iron.

Role of coordination compounds in medicinal chemistry:

Certain coordination compounds of platinum (for example, cis-platin) are used to inhibit the growth of tumours.

Role of coordination compounds in analytical chemistry:

During salt analysis, many basic radicals are detected using the colour changes they show with different reagents. These colour changes happen because the basic radicals form coordination compounds, or complexes, with different ligands.

Role of coordination compounds in extraction or metallurgy of metals:

Extracting some metals from their ores involves forming complexes. For example, in aqueous solution, gold combines with cyanide ions to form $\left[\mathrm{Au}(\mathrm{CN})_{2}\right]$. Gold is later extracted from this solution by adding zinc metal.
